14204.m: The retiarius fought with a net and a trident.

a: Slaves, prisoners of war and convicts
14205.e: Most gladiators were unfree people who were trained in gladiator schools. But there were also volunteers who hoped for fame and money.

14206.q: What did a gladiator receive as a sign that he no longer had to fight in the arena?
14206.e: The wooden sword or wooden staff was called a “rudis”. Whoever received it was released from fighting in the arena.
14206.m: With the wooden sword, a gladiator was released from the arena.

14207.q: What do you call the sand-covered fighting area in an amphitheatre?
14207.e: “Arena” means sand in Latin. The sand soaked up blood and gave the fighters a firm footing.
14207.m: The arena gets its name from the Latin word for sand.

14208.q: How did most people in the Roman Empire become slaves?
14208.e: During conquests the Romans captured many people and sold them at slave markets. Pirates and human traffickers also sold captives.
14208.m: Many slaves in the Roman Empire were prisoners of war.

14209.q: What was the legal status of slaves in the Roman Empire?
a: They were seen as the property of their owners
They were citizens with the right to vote
14209.e: Slaves had hardly any rights and could be sold. How well or badly they were treated depended a lot on their owner and their work.
14209.m: Roman slaves were seen as property and had hardly any rights.

14210.q: How could a slave in the Roman Empire sometimes gain their freedom?
a: By being freed, often in return for payment
14210.e: Owners could free slaves, sometimes only in their will. Some slaves bought their freedom with their savings and were then called freedmen, in Latin liberti.
14210.m: Roman slaves could be freed or buy their freedom.

14211.q: Where did slaves in the Roman Empire have to work in especially harsh conditions?
14211.e: In mines and quarries the work was hard and dangerous. Many slaves died young there.
14211.m: Work in the mines was especially hard for slaves.

14212.q: What job did educated slaves, often from Greece, have in rich Roman families?
14212.e: Many private tutors in Rome were educated Greek slaves. They taught the children reading, writing and Greek.
14212.m: Educated slaves in Rome often worked as private tutors.

14213.q: At which festival in December were slaves in Rome allowed to celebrate almost like free people for a short time?
14213.e: During the Saturnalia the rules were relaxed for a few days. Masters and slaves sometimes ate together, and afterwards the old order applied again.
14213.m: During the Saturnalia the rules for slaves were briefly relaxed.

14214.q: What was the status of children of an enslaved woman in the Roman Empire?
14214.e: Under Roman law, a child's status followed the mother's. Children of an enslaved woman were therefore unfree from birth.
14214.m: In Rome, children of an enslaved woman were unfree from birth.

14215.q: According to the Gospels, under which Roman governor was Jesus crucified?
14215.e: Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of the province of Judaea. According to the Gospels, he sentenced Jesus to death on the cross.
14215.m: Jesus was crucified under the governor Pontius Pilate.

14216.q: Which apostle spread Christianity on many journeys through the Roman Empire?
14216.e: Paul travelled through Asia Minor and Greece and founded Christian communities. His letters are in the New Testament.
14216.m: The apostle Paul spread Christianity in the Roman Empire.

14217.q: Why were Christians persecuted at times in the Roman Empire?
a: They refused to worship the emperor as a god
They did not want to pay taxes
14217.e: Christians believed in only one God and refused to make sacrifices for the emperor. This was seen as a danger to the state, so they were persecuted at times.
14217.m: Christians were persecuted because they rejected the worship of the emperor.

14218.q: Which emperor allowed Christians to practise their faith freely in AD 313 with the Edict of Milan?
14218.e: Constantine the Great and his co-emperor Licinius granted freedom to all religions. Christians could now practise their faith openly and got back property that had been seized.
14218.m: Emperor Constantine allowed the Christian faith in AD 313.

14219.q: What did Christianity become in the Roman Empire in AD 380?
14219.e: Emperor Theodosius I declared Christianity the official religion of the empire. Old cults were then banned bit by bit.
14219.m: In AD 380 Christianity became the state religion.

14220.q: Which animal is seen as an early symbol of the Christians?
14220.e: The Greek word for fish, “Ichthys”, was read as an abbreviation for “Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour”. So the fish became a Christian symbol.
14220.m: The fish was an early symbol of the Christians.

14221.q: According to legend, who was Saint Maurice, after whom the town of Saint-Maurice in Valais is named?
14221.e: According to legend, Maurice was the leader of the Theban Legion. He and his soldiers died because, as Christians, they did not want to fight against Christians. Whether this really happened is not certain.
14221.m: According to legend, Saint Maurice was a Christian soldier.

14222.q: According to legend, which saints are the patron saints of Zurich?
14222.e: According to legend, Felix and Regula were executed in Zurich for being Christians. Whether they really lived is not certain.
14222.m: According to legend, Felix and Regula are the patron saints of Zurich.

14223.q: Which group of peoples did the Helvetii belong to?
14223.e: The Helvetii were a Celtic tribe in the Swiss Plateau. They lived in villages and fortified settlements called oppida.
14223.m: The Helvetii were a Celtic people.

14224.q: Who defeated the Helvetii at Bibracte in Gaul in 58 BC?
14224.e: The Helvetii wanted to move to south-western Gaul. Caesar stood in their way and defeated them at Bibracte.
14224.m: Caesar defeated the Helvetii at Bibracte in 58 BC.

14225.q: What did Caesar order the Helvetii to do after their defeat at Bibracte?
14225.e: Caesar sent the survivors back to their old area of settlement. That way the land would not stay empty and would not be taken over by Germanic tribes.
14225.m: After Bibracte, the Helvetii had to return to their homeland.

14226.q: Where did the Helvetii want to move to in 58 BC?
14226.e: The Helvetii burned their villages and wanted to move to south-western Gaul in today's France. Caesar stood in their way and defeated them at Bibracte.
14226.m: The Helvetii wanted to move to south-western Gaul.

14227.q: What does the abbreviation “CH” for Switzerland stand for?
14227.e: “Confoederatio Helvetica” is Latin and means “Helvetic Confederation”. The name recalls the Helvetii.
14227.m: The abbreviation CH stands for Confoederatio Helvetica.

14228.q: Against whom did the Helvetii win a great victory in 107 BC?
14228.e: The leader Divico and a group of Helvetii defeated a Roman army in south-western Gaul. Caesar later mentions this victory in his account.
14228.m: The Helvetii defeated a Roman army in 107 BC.

14229.q: What was today's city of Zurich called in Roman times?
14229.e: Turicum was a Roman customs post on the Limmat. A gravestone with this name was found on the Lindenhof in 1747.
14229.m: In Roman times Zurich was called Turicum.

14230.q: What was today's city of Geneva called in Roman times?
14230.e: Genava lay where the Rhône flows out of Lake Geneva. Caesar already mentions the place in his account of the Gallic War.
14230.m: In Roman times Geneva was called Genava.

14231.q: Near which of today's municipalities are the ruins of Augusta Raurica?
14231.e: Augusta Raurica lies east of Basel on the Rhine. Augst belongs to the canton of Basel-Landschaft, Kaiseraugst to the canton of Aargau.
14231.m: Augusta Raurica lies near Augst and Kaiseraugst.

14232.q: Which people founded the town of Augusta Raurica?
14232.e: Augusta Raurica was a Roman colony on the Rhine. The name honours Emperor Augustus and the Celtic tribe of the Rauraci.
14232.m: Augusta Raurica was a Roman town.

14233.q: Which people is Augusta Raurica named after?
14233.e: The Rauraci were a Celtic tribe in the area around Basel. “Augusta” also honours Emperor Augustus.
14233.m: Augusta Raurica bears the name of the Celtic tribe of the Rauraci.

14234.q: Roughly how many people lived in Augusta Raurica at its height?
14234.e: For its height around AD 200, experts estimate between about 10,000 and 20,000 inhabitants. That made it an important Roman town north of the Alps.
14234.m: At its height, Augusta Raurica probably had 10,000 to 20,000 inhabitants.

14235.q: Which famous find was discovered in Augusta Raurica in 1961 and 1962?
14235.e: The treasure includes about 270 objects made from about 58 kilograms of silver, such as plates, bowls and coins. It was buried around AD 350, but nobody knows for sure why.
14235.m: An important late Roman silver treasure was found in Augusta Raurica.

14236.q: Which large building in Augusta Raurica is still used for performances today?
14236.e: The Roman theatre of Augusta Raurica held several thousand spectators. It has been restored and is used again today as a venue for concerts and performances.
14236.m: Performances are held again today in the Roman theatre of Augusta Raurica.

14237.q: What did the Romans build right on the Rhine near Augusta Raurica around AD 300 to protect the border?
14237.e: After attacks and destruction in the 3rd century, the Castrum Rauracense was built right on the Rhine. It guarded the border against the Alemanni.
14237.m: The Castrum Rauracense guarded the Rhine border.

14238.q: What is the name of today's small town where the Roman town of Aventicum used to be?
14238.e: Avenches is in the canton of Vaud, near Lake Murten. Many remains of the Roman town can be seen there.
14238.m: The Roman town of Aventicum was at today's Avenches.

14239.q: What was the importance of Aventicum for the Helvetii in Roman times?
14239.e: Aventicum was the main town of the civitas of the Helvetii. The administration of the Helvetian territory was organised here.
14239.m: Aventicum was the main town of the Helvetii in Roman times.

14240.q: Which Roman building can still be clearly seen in Avenches today?
14240.e: The amphitheatre of Aventicum held thousands of spectators. Today concerts and festivals take place there again.
14240.m: The Roman amphitheatre still stands in Avenches.

14241.q: Which gold find was discovered in Aventicum in 1939?
a: A bust of Emperor Marcus Aurelius
14241.e: The golden bust of Marcus Aurelius was found in a drain near a temple. Today it is one of the best-known Roman finds in Switzerland.
14241.m: A golden bust of Marcus Aurelius was found in Aventicum in 1939.

14242.q: Roughly how long was the town wall of Aventicum?
14242.e: The town wall was a good 5 kilometres long and had 73 towers. It enclosed a much larger area than was actually lived in.
14242.m: The town wall of Aventicum was several kilometres long.

14243.q: Which bird is the tall Roman column “Cigognier” in Avenches named after?
14243.e: The French word for stork is “cigogne”. Storks used to nest on top of the temple column, which is about 12 metres high.
14243.m: The Cigognier is named after the storks that nested on the column.

14244.q: Next to which Roman building in Aventicum does the medieval tower with the Roman Museum stand?
14244.e: Above the main entrance of the amphitheatre stands a medieval tower that houses the Roman Museum. For a long time there was an opera festival in the amphitheatre; today there are concerts and festivals.
14244.m: The Roman Museum stands at the amphitheatre of Aventicum.

14245.q: In which year did the Western Roman Empire end with the removal of its last emperor?
14245.e: In this year, a Germanic military leader removed the last emperor in Italy and did not appoint a new one. This year is seen as the end of the Western Roman Empire.
14245.m: The Western Roman Empire ended in AD 476.

14246.q: What was the name of the last emperor of the Western Roman Empire?
14246.e: Romulus Augustulus was still a teenager when he was removed from power. His name recalls the city's founder Romulus and the first emperor Augustus.
14246.m: Romulus Augustulus was the last Western Roman emperor.

14247.q: Which Germanic military leader removed the last Western Roman emperor?
14247.e: Odoacer then took over rule in Italy himself. He sent the imperial insignia to the emperor in the Eastern Roman Empire.
14247.m: Odoacer removed the last Western Roman emperor.

14248.q: Into which two parts was the Roman Empire finally divided in AD 395?
14248.e: After the emperor's death, each of his two sons received one half of the empire. From then on, the Western and Eastern Empires developed separately.
14248.m: After 395 there was a Western Roman Empire and an Eastern Roman Empire.

14249.q: Which people under King Alaric plundered the city of Rome in AD 410?
14249.e: The plundering of Rome by the Visigoths shocked people throughout the empire. Rome had not been captured by enemies for about 800 years.
14249.m: The Visigoths under Alaric plundered Rome in AD 410.

14250.q: What are the great movements of Germanic and other peoples that weakened the Western Roman Empire called?
14250.e: From the late 4th century, many peoples pushed into the Roman Empire, partly because the Huns were driving them out of the east. The empire could hardly protect its borders any more.
14250.m: The Migration Period contributed to the fall of Western Rome.

14251.q: Which Germanic people settled mainly in northern and eastern Switzerland after the end of Roman rule?
14251.e: The Alemanni brought their Germanic language with them. Swiss German developed from it, while in western Switzerland the Burgundians took over the Latin language.
14251.m: The Alemanni shaped German-speaking Switzerland after Roman times.

14252.q: Until when did the Eastern Roman Empire continue?
14252.e: The Eastern Roman or Byzantine Empire outlived Western Rome by almost 1000 years. In 1453 the Ottomans conquered its capital.

14253.q: In which year was Charlemagne crowned emperor in Rome?
14253.e: On Christmas Day in the year 800, Charles was crowned emperor by the Pope in Rome. This meant there was once again an emperor in the West, as in the old Roman Empire.
14253.m: Charlemagne was crowned emperor in Rome in the year 800.

14254.e: Pope Leo III placed the imperial crown on Charles’s head in St Peter’s in Rome. Charles had earlier supported the Pope against opponents in Rome.
14254.m: Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor.

14255.q: In which city did Charlemagne most like to stay in his later years?
14255.e: Charles had no fixed capital but travelled with his court from palace to palace. In his later years he mostly lived at the palace of Aachen, where he is also buried.

14256.q: Against which people did Charlemagne wage war for around 30 years?
14256.e: The Saxon Wars lasted from 772 to 804. Charles conquered the Saxons and forced them to accept Christianity.
14256.m: Charlemagne fought the Saxons for around 30 years.

14257.q: What were the envoys called whom Charlemagne used to check on the counts in his empire?
14257.e: The king’s envoys (in Latin missi dominici) usually travelled through the empire in pairs. They checked whether the counts followed the king’s orders and judged fairly.
14257.m: King’s envoys checked on the counts on Charles’s behalf.

14258.q: Which easy-to-read script developed in the time of Charlemagne?
14258.e: In the writing rooms of the Carolingian empire, Carolingian minuscule developed, with clear small letters. Our lower-case letters today go back to this script.
14258.m: Our lower-case letters come from Carolingian minuscule.

14259.q: According to a legend, what did Charlemagne found in Zurich?
14259.e: According to a legend, Charlemagne found the graves of the city’s saints Felix and Regula while hunting and founded the Grossmünster there. This story is not historically proven.
14259.m: According to legend, Charlemagne founded Zurich’s Grossmünster.

14260.q: Which Frankish king was baptised as a Christian around 500?
14260.e: The Merovingian Clovis I united the Franks and was baptised around 500. This made the Frankish kingdom a Christian kingdom.
14260.m: Clovis I made the Franks Christians.

14261.q: Which people, who also settled in today’s German-speaking Switzerland, were defeated by the Frankish king around 500?
14261.e: The Frankish king defeated the Alemanni around 496, and decisively again in 506. After that they gradually came under Frankish rule.
14261.m: Around 500, the Franks defeated the Alemanni.

14262.q: What office did Charles Martel and Pepin hold at the court of the Merovingian kings?
14262.e: The mayor of the palace originally ran the royal court. Over time, the mayors of the palace had more power than the Merovingian kings themselves.
14262.m: The mayors of the palace were the real rulers in the late Merovingian kingdom.

14263.q: Which Carolingian became the first of his family to be King of the Franks in 751?
14263.e: In 751, with the Pope’s approval, Pepin the Short removed the last Merovingian king. He was the father of Charlemagne.
14263.m: Pepin the Short was the first Carolingian king.

14264.q: Whom did Charles Martel fight in 732 at the Battle of Tours and Poitiers?
14264.e: In 732, Charles Martel defeated an Arab army that had pushed north from Spain. The Arabs withdrew, but smaller battles in the south of France went on for years.
14264.m: In 732, Charles Martel stopped an Arab army in the Frankish kingdom.

14265.q: What happened to the Frankish empire in the Treaty of Verdun in 843?
a: It was divided into three parts
14265.e: Charlemagne’s three grandsons divided the empire among themselves. The western part later became France, and the eastern part developed into what later became Germany.
14265.m: The Treaty of Verdun divided the Frankish empire into three parts in 843.

14266.q: Which region did the Vikings come from?
14266.e: The Vikings came from what is now Norway, Sweden and Denmark. This region is called Scandinavia.

14267.q: Which place was raided by Vikings in 793, an event seen as the start of the Viking Age?
14267.e: In 793, Vikings raided the monastery of Lindisfarne on the coast of England. This event is seen as the start of the Viking Age.
14267.m: The raid on Lindisfarne in 793 began the Viking Age.

14268.q: What are the fast, narrow ships of the Vikings called?
14268.e: Longships sat shallow in the water and could be sailed and rowed. That way the Vikings crossed the sea and also travelled up rivers.
14268.m: The Vikings travelled across seas and rivers in longships.

14269.q: Which Viking reached North America around the year 1000?
14269.e: Leif Erikson sailed from Greenland to North America and called the land Vinland. Remains of a Viking settlement have been found in Newfoundland.
14269.m: Leif Erikson reached America around 500 years before Columbus.

14270.q: Which region in France is named after the Vikings?
14270.e: In the year 911, the Viking leader Rollo received land on the Seine from the French king. The area was named Normandy after the “Northmen”.
14270.m: Normandy takes its name from the Northmen.

14271.q: Which god was the father of the gods in the Viking religion?
14271.e: The Vikings believed in many gods. Odin was seen as the father of the gods, and his son Thor as the god of thunder.
14271.m: Odin was the chief god of the Vikings.

14272.q: Which island in the North Atlantic did the Vikings settle from about 870 onwards?
14272.e: Settlers from Norway made their home in Iceland from about 870. There, in 930, the Althing was founded, one of the oldest parliaments in the world.
14272.m: From about 870, Vikings settled the island of Iceland.

14273.q: Which stages of training did a boy go through to become a knight?
14273.e: At about seven, a noble’s son went to another lord’s court as a page. At about 14 he became a knight’s squire, and usually at around 21 a knight himself.
14273.m: A future knight was first a page and then a squire.

14274.q: What was the solemn ceremony called in which a squire was admitted to knighthood?
14274.e: When he was girded with the sword, the squire received his sword and so became a knight. Later people also spoke of the accolade, or dubbing.
14274.m: Girding with the sword turned a squire into a knight.

14275.q: What were the fighting contests called in which knights showed their skill?
14275.e: At tournaments, knights fought each other on horseback with lances. They practised for war and could win fame and prizes.
14275.m: At tournaments, knights competed in combat.

14276.q: What were the knights’ coats of arms for?
14276.e: Under helmet and armour, knights could hardly be recognised. The coat of arms on the shield showed who was hidden underneath.
14276.m: You could recognise a knight in full armour by his coat of arms.

14277.q: What are the love songs called that knights performed for noble ladies at court?
14277.e: In Minnesang, poets sang of their devotion to a noble lady. It was part of the courtly culture of the age of knights.
14277.m: Minnesang was the courtly love poetry of the knights.

14278.q: What did knights’ protective clothing mainly consist of in the High Middle Ages?
14278.e: Chain mail was made of thousands of small iron rings. Full suits of armour made of iron plates only became common in the late Middle Ages, especially in the 15th century.
14278.m: In the High Middle Ages, knights mainly wore chain mail.

14279.q: Where did the Swiss Confederates defeat a Habsburg army of knights in 1315?
14279.e: At Morgarten, the Confederates ambushed the Habsburg army in a narrow pass. The heavily armoured knights could hardly defend themselves there.
14279.m: At Morgarten in 1315, the Confederates defeated Habsburg knights.

14280.q: What is the tallest and strongest tower of a castle called?
14280.e: The keep was usually the tallest tower of the castle. It served as a lookout and showed the lord’s power; it may also have been a last refuge during attacks.
14280.m: The keep was the main tower of a castle.

14281.q: What is the residential building with the knights’ hall in a castle called?
14281.e: The lord’s family lived in the palas. The great hall for feasts and receptions was also here.
14281.m: The lord’s family lived in the palas.

14283.q: What was a drawbridge at a castle for?
14283.e: The drawbridge led across the moat to the gate. When there was danger, it was pulled up so that attackers could not reach the gate.
14283.m: The drawbridge could block the way to the castle gate.

14284.q: In which present-day canton is Habsburg Castle, the ancestral seat of the Habsburgs?
14284.e: Habsburg Castle was built in the 11th century near Brugg, in what is now the canton of Aargau. The Habsburg family named itself after it.
14284.m: The ancestral castle of the Habsburgs is in Aargau.

14286.q: Why were many castles built on mountains or rocks?
14286.e: On high ground you could see enemies early, and attackers had to fight uphill. Such castles are called hilltop castles.
14286.m: Hilltop castles were especially well protected.

14287.q: What was a fief in the Middle Ages?
a: Land lent in return for loyalty and service
14287.e: A lord let a follower use land or rights. But the land still belonged to the lord.
14287.m: A fief was land granted in return for loyalty and service.

14288.q: What do you call someone who received a fief from a lord?
14288.e: The vassal was the one who held the fief, and the lord was called the liege lord. Both were bound by mutual loyalty.
14288.m: A vassal received a fief from his liege lord.

14289.q: Who was at the top of the feudal pyramid?
14289.e: The king granted fiefs to dukes, counts and bishops. They in turn passed parts of them on to lesser vassals.
14289.m: The king was at the top of the feudal pyramid.

14290.q: What did a vassal mainly have to provide for his lord?
a: Years of travel as a journeyman
14290.e: The vassal had to come to his lord’s aid with armed fighters. He also owed him advice and loyalty.
14290.m: Vassals mainly owed their lord military service.

14291.q: What did the liege lord promise his vassal in return for his loyalty?
a: Freedom from dues to the Church
14291.e: The feudal relationship was based on give and take. The lord gave land and protection, the vassal loyalty and service.
14291.m: The liege lord owed his vassal protection.

14292.q: How did fiefs change over the course of the Middle Ages?
14292.e: Originally a fief went back to the lord when the vassal died. Over time, however, the sons inherited the fief, which strengthened the power of the nobility.

14293.q: According to medieval thinking, which three estates of society were there?
14293.e: According to this idea, each of the three estates had its own task, willed by God. That is why people thought this order was right and could not be changed.
14293.m: Society was made up of clergy, nobility and peasants.

14294.q: According to the order of estates, what was the task of the nobility?
14294.e: The nobility was the estate of those who fight. It was meant to protect the other estates with weapons.
14294.m: The nobility had the task of protecting the others.

14295.q: In the Middle Ages, how did people usually become members of an estate?
14295.e: Anyone born the child of peasants usually remained a peasant all their life. Rising in society was rare, and most likely by joining the Church.
14295.m: Your estate was usually decided by birth.

14296.q: Which estate made up the great majority of the population?
14296.e: By far most people in the Middle Ages lived in the countryside and worked in farming. The nobility and clergy were only a small minority.
14296.m: Most people in the Middle Ages were peasants.

14297.q: Because they fed everyone, what were the peasants often called?
14297.e: With their work in the fields, the peasants produced food for everyone. That is why they were called the estate that feeds.
14297.m: The peasants formed the estate that feeds.

14298.q: Which group no longer fitted well into the old three-part order of estates in the late Middle Ages?
14298.e: As towns grew, craftsmen and merchants emerged as self-confident citizens. They were neither nobility nor clergy nor peasants.
14298.m: Town citizens broke up the old order of estates.

14299.q: What do you call peasants who were unfree and bound to their lord?
14299.e: Serfs could not simply leave their farm and often needed the lord’s permission to marry. They had to pay dues and provide services.
14299.m: Serfs were bound to their lord.

a: A payment of a tenth of the harvest to the Church
Ten days of work for the king
Ten silver coins for the knight
A tenth of the land for the town
14300.e: The tithe was a payment of about a tenth of what was produced. It went to the Church and was a heavy burden for peasants.
14300.m: The tithe was a payment to the Church.

14301.q: What did labour service mean for a peasant?
a: Military service in the king’s army
Working as a monk in a monastery
14301.e: In labour service, peasants had to work on the lord’s fields or do carting on certain days. They received no pay for it.
14301.m: Labour service was unpaid work for the landlord.

14302.q: What is special about the three-field system?
a: One field is left fallow each year
The land is ploughed three times a year
14302.e: The farmland was divided into three parts: winter grain, summer grain and fallow land. This let the soil recover, and the harvests became bigger.
14302.m: In the three-field system, a third of the land rested each year.

14303.q: What is land called that all the farmers in a village were allowed to use together?
14303.e: Meadows, pastures and woods were often common land. In Switzerland, such shared commons (Allmenden) still exist today.
14303.m: The common land belonged to the whole village community.

14304.q: What is a lord’s rule over land and the peasants who farmed it called?
14304.e: The lord of the manor owned the land and gave it to peasants to farm. In return he demanded dues and services and often also had the right to judge them.
14304.m: Under manorialism, peasants farmed a lord’s land.

14305.q: What does the saying “town air makes you free” mean?
a: Runaway serfs could become free in a town
The air in town was cleaner
Anyone could enter the town for free
14305.e: A runaway serf who lived in a town for a year and a day without being taken back was often regarded as free. That is why many peasants were drawn to the towns.
14305.m: Town air made you free because serfs could become free in a town.

14306.q: Which noble family founded the towns of Bern and Fribourg in the 12th century?
14306.e: The Dukes of Zähringen founded several towns in the 12th century, including Fribourg and Bern. They wanted to secure their rule this way.
14306.m: The Zähringens founded the towns of Bern and Fribourg.

14307.q: According to tradition, in which year was Bern founded?
14307.e: According to tradition, Bern was founded in 1191 in a loop of the River Aare. The river protected the town on three sides.
14307.m: According to tradition, Bern was founded in 1191.

14308.q: Which right was especially important for a medieval town to be able to trade?
14308.e: With market rights, markets could be held regularly in the town. Traders and farmers from the surrounding area came to buy and sell goods.
14308.m: Market rights brought trade and wealth to the town.

a: The farmers from the surrounding area
14309.e: In many towns, the citizens decided their own affairs. At the top were a council and a mayor or chief magistrate.
14309.m: Many towns were governed by a council of citizens.

14310.q: Why were medieval towns surrounded by walls?
a: So that the cows didn’t run away
14310.e: The town wall protected citizens and their goods from enemies. At the gates, people could control who came in and collect tolls.
14310.m: Town walls protected the citizens from enemies.

a: An association of craftsmen in one trade
14311.e: In a guild, for example, all the bakers or blacksmiths of a town joined together. The guild set rules on prices, quality and training.
14311.m: A guild united craftsmen of the same trade.

14312.q: Which stages did a craftsman go through in the guild?
14312.e: An apprentice learned the craft from a master. As a journeyman he worked for wages, and only as a master could he run his own workshop.
14312.m: A craftsman was first an apprentice, then a journeyman and finally a master.

14313.q: What did a journeyman have to make in order to become a master?
14313.e: With his masterpiece, a journeyman proved his skill. The masters of the guild checked whether it was good enough.
14313.m: With his masterpiece, a journeyman showed his skill.

14314.q: What is the building called where the members of a guild met?
14314.e: Guild members met in the guildhall for meetings, meals and celebrations. Zurich still has several historic guildhalls today.
14314.m: Guild members gathered in the guildhall.

14315.q: What did compulsory guild membership mean?
a: Only guild members were allowed to practise the trade
Every citizen had to learn a trade
Guilds had to pay taxes to the king
14315.e: Anyone who wanted to practise a trade in the town had to be a member of the guild. This way the guilds protected their members from competition.
14315.m: Because of compulsory guild membership, only guild members could practise the trade.

14316.q: Who introduced a constitution in Zurich in 1336 that gave the guilds a say in the council?
14316.e: In 1336, Rudolf Brun overthrew the old council and became mayor. His constitution gave the craftsmen’s guilds seats on Zurich’s town council.
14316.m: In 1336, Rudolf Brun gave Zurich’s guilds power on the council.

14317.q: Which Zurich spring festival still recalls the guilds today?
14317.e: At Sechseläuten, the Zurich guilds parade through the city in historical costumes. At the end, the Böögg is burned.
14317.m: At Sechseläuten, the Zurich guilds parade through the city.

14318.q: Who was the head of the Catholic Church in the Middle Ages?
14318.e: The Pope in Rome was the head of the Western Church. He claimed great power, even over kings and emperors.
14318.m: The Pope in Rome led the Church.

14319.q: Which king went to Canossa as a penitent in 1077 to ask the Pope for forgiveness?
14319.e: Henry IV had got into a serious quarrel with Pope Gregory VII and had been excommunicated by him, and many princes turned against him. In winter he crossed the Alps to Canossa and got the Pope to forgive him.
14319.m: In 1077, Henry IV went to Canossa to ask the Pope for forgiveness.

14320.q: What was the Investiture Controversy about?
a: Who was allowed to appoint bishops
Who was allowed to build castles
14320.e: The Emperor and the Pope argued about who was allowed to install bishops in their office. The word investiture means installing someone in an office.
14320.m: The Investiture Controversy was about appointing bishops.

14321.q: What did it mean when the Pope excommunicated someone?
14321.e: Excommunication shut a person out of the community of the Church. For a king this was dangerous, because his subjects then no longer had to obey him.
14321.m: Excommunication shut a person out of the Church.

14322.q: In which language were church services held in the West in the Middle Ages?
14322.e: Latin was the language of the Church and of scholars. That is why most ordinary people did not understand the services.
14322.m: The Western Church held its services in Latin.

14323.q: How can you recognise a church in the Gothic style?
a: A dome and a hall of columns
A flat roof and small windows
14323.e: The Gothic style began in France in the 12th century. With pointed arches and buttresses, very tall churches with large stained-glass windows could be built.
14323.m: Gothic churches have pointed arches and tall windows.

14325.q: What was the room in a monastery called where monks copied books by hand?
14325.e: In the scriptorium, monks copied books onto parchment with quill and ink. Many books were also beautifully decorated.
14325.m: Monks copied books in the scriptorium.

14326.q: Who led a monastery for men?
14326.e: The abbot was elected by the monks and led the monastery. A convent for women was led by an abbess.

14327.q: Which famous Swiss monastery was founded in 934 and is an important place of pilgrimage?
14327.e: The Benedictine monastery of Einsiedeln was founded in 934 at the place where the hermit Meinrad had lived. To this day, many people make pilgrimages to the Black Madonna.
14327.m: Einsiedeln has been an important place of pilgrimage since the Middle Ages.

14328.q: Which monastery complex with a famous abbey library is a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
14328.e: The Abbey of St Gallen was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1983. The abbey library owns valuable medieval manuscripts.
14328.m: The Abbey of St Gallen is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

14329.q: Which saint founded an order in the 13th century that lived in poverty and preached?
14329.e: Francis of Assisi gave up his wealth and lived in poverty. His order, the Franciscans, is one of the mendicant orders, which worked mainly in towns.
14329.m: Francis of Assisi founded the Franciscan order.

14330.q: Which pope called for the First Crusade in 1095?
14330.e: In 1095, Pope Urban II called for a crusade at Clermont in France. Thousands of knights and ordinary people answered the call.
14330.m: Urban II called for the First Crusade in 1095.

14331.q: Which city was the most important goal of the Crusades?
14331.e: The crusaders wanted to conquer Jerusalem and the holy places of Christianity. The city is also holy to Jews and Muslims.
14331.m: Jerusalem was the main goal of the Crusades.

14332.q: In which year did the crusaders capture Jerusalem in the First Crusade?
14332.e: In 1099 the crusaders took Jerusalem. In doing so they killed many of the city’s inhabitants, both Muslims and Jews.

14333.q: Where do the Crusades get their name from?
a: From the cross on their clothing
14333.e: The participants sewed a cloth cross onto their clothing. This showed that they had taken a vow to go on the expedition.
14333.m: Crusaders wore a cross on their clothing.

14334.q: Which sultan took Jerusalem back from the crusaders in 1187?
14334.e: Saladin defeated the crusaders in 1187 and took Jerusalem. Even his Christian enemies saw him as a chivalrous ruler.

14335.q: Which communities of monks who also fought were founded during the Crusades?
14335.e: Military orders such as the Templars or the Knights Hospitaller combined monastic life and fighting. They protected pilgrims and cared for the sick.
14335.m: In military orders, knights lived like monks.

14336.q: What happened in 1291 to the crusaders’ rule in the Holy Land?
a: It spread as far as Egypt
It was banned by the Pope
14336.e: With the fall of the fortress of Acre in 1291, the crusaders’ rule in the Holy Land ended.
14336.m: In 1291 the age of the crusaders in the Holy Land ended.

14337.q: Around what time did the great wave of plague, the Black Death, rage in Europe?
14337.e: The plague reached Europe in 1347 on trading ships and spread across almost the whole continent within a few years. It reached Switzerland in 1348 and 1349.
14337.m: The Black Death raged in Europe around 1350.

14338.q: Roughly what share of Europe’s population died of the Black Death?
14338.e: Estimates range from a quarter to half of the population; around a third is often given. Some places were almost empty afterwards.
14338.m: About a third of the people in Europe died of the Black Death.

14339.q: How was the plague mainly passed on to people?
14339.e: Fleas sucked blood from sick rats and then bit people. Pneumonic plague was also passed directly from person to person, and human fleas and lice probably played a part too.
14339.m: Rat fleas passed the plague on to people.

14340.q: Which group of people was wrongly accused of poisoning the wells during the plague?
14340.e: Many people looked for someone to blame for the epidemic and spread false rumours about Jews. In many towns, including Basel and Zurich, Jewish communities were persecuted and murdered.
14340.m: During the plague, Jews were wrongly blamed and persecuted.

14341.q: Where does the word “quarantine” come from?
a: From the name of a doctor
From the Latin word for illness
14341.e: The word comes from the Italian “quaranta”, meaning 40. Ships and travellers in port cities such as Venice had to wait 40 days before they were allowed to enter the city.
14341.m: Quarantine originally meant a waiting period of 40 days.

14342.q: What effect did the Black Death have on the surviving workers and peasants?
a: Workers became scarce and more in demand
Suddenly there were too many workers
The towns immediately grew a lot
14342.e: Because so many people had died, there was a shortage of workers. Many survivors could therefore demand higher wages or better conditions.
14342.m: After the plague, workers were scarce and valuable.

14343.q: Who invented printing with movable type in Europe around 1450?
14343.e: Gutenberg developed a printing method using single metal letters. With it, books could be made much faster than by hand.
14343.m: Johannes Gutenberg invented printing with movable type around 1450.

14344.q: In which city was the printing workshop where Gutenberg printed his famous Bible?
14344.e: Gutenberg came from Mainz and, after years in Strasbourg, set up his printing workshop there. Today the Gutenberg Museum in Mainz remembers him.
14344.m: Gutenberg printed his books in Mainz.

14345.q: What was new about Gutenberg’s invention?
a: Single letters that could be rearranged
14345.e: Gutenberg cast single letters out of metal, known as type. They could be rearranged for each page and used again and again.
14345.m: Movable type could be set again and again.

14346.q: Roughly how many copies of the Gutenberg Bible were printed?
14346.e: By about 1455, Gutenberg had printed around 180 Bibles, most on paper and some on parchment. Only a few copies survive today.
14346.m: Around 180 copies of the Gutenberg Bible were printed.

14347.q: In which language did Gutenberg print his famous Bible?
14347.e: The Gutenberg Bible is printed in Latin, as was usual for Bibles in the Western Church at the time. Because most columns have 42 lines, it is also called the 42-line Bible.
14347.m: Gutenberg’s Bible was printed in Latin.

14348.q: Which Swiss city became an important centre of printing in the 15th and 16th centuries?
14348.e: Basel had a university and many scholars, which helped printing to flourish. Printers such as Johann Froben made the city famous.
14348.m: Basel was an important printing city.

14349.q: What effect did printing have on the spread of knowledge?
a: Books became cheaper and spread faster
Only monks were allowed to read
Books became more expensive than before
There were fewer books than before
14349.e: With printing, many identical copies could be made. Books and pamphlets became cheaper, and new ideas such as those of the Reformation spread quickly.
14349.m: Printing spread knowledge faster and more cheaply.

14350.q: In which present-day canton is the ancestral castle of the Habsburgs?
14350.e: Habsburg Castle stands on the Wülpelsberg in the municipality of Habsburg in the canton of Aargau. The noble family takes its name from this castle.
14350.m: The Habsburgs originally come from Aargau.

14351.q: About how old is Habsburg Castle in Aargau?
14351.e: Count Radbot had the castle built around 1020/1030. The oldest part is a stone house from that time.
14351.m: Habsburg Castle was built about 1000 years ago.

14352.q: What did the early Habsburgs found in Muri in Aargau in 1027?
14352.e: Radbot and his wife Ita of Lorraine founded Muri Abbey in 1027. It became an important family monastery of the early Habsburgs.
14352.m: Muri Abbey was founded by the early Habsburgs.

14353.q: What did Count Rudolf of Habsburg become in 1273?
14353.e: Count Rudolf of Habsburg became King of the Holy Roman Empire in 1273. With this, the Habsburgs rose to become one of the most powerful families in Europe.
14353.m: With Rudolf I, the Habsburgs became kings in 1273.

14354.q: What happened to the Habsburg king Albert I near Windisch in 1308?
a: He founded the town of Zurich
He made peace with the Confederates
14354.e: King Albert I was murdered by his nephew John near Windisch on 1 May 1308. Königsfelden Abbey was later built at the scene.
14354.m: King Albert I was murdered near Windisch in 1308.

14355.q: Which area did the Habsburgs lose to the Confederates in 1415?
14355.e: In 1415, Bern and other Confederate places conquered Aargau. With this, the Habsburgs also finally lost their ancestral castle.
14355.m: Since 1415, Aargau has no longer belonged to the Habsburgs.

14356.q: What were the officials called who ran an area on behalf of a lord and acted as judges there?
14356.e: A bailiff ran an area for his lord, collected dues and acted as judge. In the Tell legend, Gessler is such a bailiff.
14356.m: A bailiff governed an area in the name of his lord.

14357.q: What did Habsburg and the Confederates agree in the “Perpetual Accord” of 1474?
14357.e: In the Perpetual Accord of 1474, Habsburg and the Confederates made a lasting peace. Both sides recognised the areas they held at the time.
14357.m: The Perpetual Accord ended the long quarrel between Habsburg and the Confederates in 1474.

14358.q: In which present-day country was the later centre of Habsburg power, with its capital Vienna?
14358.e: From 1282, the Habsburgs ruled over Austria and made Vienna the centre of their power. They ruled there until 1918.
14358.m: Later, the Habsburgs ruled from Vienna in Austria.

14359.e: The canton of Aargau took over the castle in 1804. Today there is a restaurant there and a small exhibition on the history of the Habsburgs.
14359.m: Habsburg Castle is owned by the canton of Aargau today.

14360.q: Which gorge in the canton of Uri was crossed with the Devil's Bridge?
14360.e: The Schöllenen Gorge near Andermatt was for a long time a big obstacle on the way south. Only with bridges like the Devil's Bridge did the route become easy to use in the 13th century.
14360.m: The Devil's Bridge crosses the Schöllenen Gorge in the canton of Uri.

14361.q: What is the open-air assembly of men entitled to vote called, which decided important matters in the valleys of central Switzerland?
14361.e: At the Landsgemeinde, the people of the land came together, elected their leaders and voted. It still exists today in Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden.
14361.m: At the Landsgemeinde, the people of the land decided together in the open air.

14362.q: Which lake is named after the four forest cantons?
14362.e: Until the 16th century, the lake was often called Lake Lucerne. Then the German name Vierwaldstättersee (Lake of the Four Forest Cantons) became established, after the four places around the lake.
14362.m: Lake Lucerne's German name means the lake of the four forest cantons.

14363.q: Which town was counted as the fourth forest canton from the 15th century?
14363.e: Originally, only Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden were the forest cantons. From the middle of the 15th century, people spoke of the four forest cantons including Lucerne.
14363.m: Lucerne is the fourth of the four forest cantons.

14364.q: Which Alpine pass made Uri especially important for trade in the 13th century?
14364.e: In the 13th century, the Gotthard Pass became an important trade route between north and south. Uri lay right on this route and became more important as a result.
14364.m: The Gotthard brought Uri trade and importance.

14365.q: Which valley community gave the whole of Switzerland its name?
14365.e: Schwyz acted particularly confidently towards outsiders. That is why foreigners soon called all Confederates “Schwyzer”, and this became the country's name, Switzerland.
14365.m: The name Switzerland comes from the place Schwyz.

14366.q: What did imperial immediacy mean for a valley community?
a: It was directly under the king or emperor
It never had to pay taxes again
It became a kingdom of its own
It was no longer allowed to wage war
14366.e: Imperial immediacy meant that no count or duke stood in between. The valley community was answerable only to the king or emperor.
14366.m: A valley with imperial immediacy had only the king or emperor above it.

14367.q: What was a charter of freedom (Freibrief) in the Middle Ages?
a: A love letter to the king
14367.e: With a charter of freedom, the king gave a valley community or a town special rights. In this way, Uri received imperial immediacy early on.
14367.m: A charter of freedom was a document with special rights.

14368.q: Which powerful family wanted to rule over the forest cantons in the 13th century?
14368.e: The Habsburgs owned a lot of land in what is now Switzerland. The forest cantons resisted their rule.
14368.m: The forest cantons resisted the Habsburgs.

14369.q: Into which two parts is Unterwalden divided?
14369.e: Unterwalden is made up of Obwalden and Nidwalden. The two parts are separate cantons today.
14369.m: Obwalden and Nidwalden together form Unterwalden.

14370.q: In which language is the Federal Charter of 1291 written?
14370.e: In the Middle Ages, important documents were mostly written in Latin. The Federal Charter is also written in Latin.
14370.m: The Federal Charter of 1291 is a Latin document.

14371.q: Which date is given in the Federal Charter?
14371.e: The Federal Charter gives no exact day, but “early August” 1291. That is why Switzerland celebrates its national holiday on 1 August.
14371.m: The Federal Charter dates from early August 1291.

14372.q: Where is the Federal Charter kept today?
a: In the Museum of the Swiss Charters in Schwyz
In the Federal Palace in Bern
In the National Museum in Zurich
In the town hall in Altdorf
14372.e: The original is in the Museum of the Swiss Charters of Confederation in Schwyz. The idea for it came up in 1891, and the museum opened in 1936.
14372.m: The Federal Charter can be seen in the Museum of the Swiss Charters in Schwyz.

14373.q: Which three valley communities joined together in the Federal Charter of 1291?
14373.e: In the Federal Charter, Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden form an alliance. Historians are not completely sure exactly which part of Unterwalden is meant.
14373.m: Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden made the Federal Charter in 1291.

14374.q: What did the valley communities mainly promise each other in the Federal Charter?
14374.e: The valley communities promised to help each other with advice and action against violence and attacks. The charter was an alliance for peace and security.
14374.m: In the Federal Charter, the valley communities promised to help each other.

14375.q: Which judges did the valley communities refuse to accept, according to the Federal Charter?
a: Judges who had bought their office or did not come from the valley
Judges who could not speak Latin
14375.e: The Federal Charter forbids judges who have bought their office or are not locals. That is why people often speak of the ban on “foreign judges”.
14375.m: The valley communities did not want foreign judges or judges who had bought their office.

14376.q: What did dating the parchment with the carbon-14 method show in 1992?
14376.e: The test showed an age of around 1280, probably between 1252 and 1312. This disproved the idea that the charter was only forged around 1400.
14376.m: The parchment of the Federal Charter really is from the 13th century.

14377.q: How was the Federal Charter authenticated?
14377.e: In the Middle Ages, seals made a document valid. Three seals hung from the Federal Charter, and two of them have survived.
14377.m: The Federal Charter was authenticated with seals.

14378.q: For which anniversary was 1 August celebrated for the first time in 1891?
a: 1000 years of the city of Bern
14378.e: In 1891, exactly 600 years had passed since the Federal Charter of 1291. From 1899, 1 August was celebrated every year.
14378.m: 1 August was first celebrated in 1891 for the 600th anniversary.

14379.q: Since when has 1 August been a public holiday with no work throughout Switzerland?
14379.e: In 1993, the voters accepted the 1 August initiative. Since 1994, the national holiday has been a day off work in all cantons.
14379.m: Only since 1994 has everyone in Switzerland had 1 August off.

14381.q: What do experts know about William Tell today?
a: It is not certain whether he really lived
He was a king of Uri
He became a Federal Councillor in 1291
14381.e: Tell is first mentioned in a chronicle about 180 years after 1291. That is why many people think he is a legendary figure.
14381.m: Nobody knows whether William Tell really lived.

14382.q: What were people supposed to bow to on the bailiff's orders, according to the Tell legend?
a: A flag on the town hall
14382.e: The bailiff had a hat put on a pole, and everyone had to bow to it. Tell refused and was punished.
14382.m: In the legend, Tell did not bow to the hat on the pole.

14383.q: What is the bailiff in the Tell legend called?
14383.e: In the legend, Gessler is the Habsburg bailiff. He forces Tell to shoot the apple.
14383.m: The wicked bailiff in the Tell legend is called Gessler.

14385.q: Where does Tell lie in wait for the bailiff Gessler, according to the legend?
a: In the Hohle Gasse near Küssnacht
14385.e: In the legend, Tell shoots Gessler in the Hohle Gasse, a sunken lane near Küssnacht. Before that, he had escaped at the Tellsplatte during a storm on the lake.
14385.m: The legend ends with Gessler's death in the Hohle Gasse.

14386.q: Which writer wrote the famous drama “William Tell” in 1804?
14386.e: Friedrich Schiller wrote the play in 1804. He was the first to give Tell's son the name Walter; in the older sources the son has no name.
14386.m: Friedrich Schiller made Tell world-famous with his drama.

14387.q: Which composer wrote the opera “Guillaume Tell” in 1829?
14387.e: Gioachino Rossini set the Tell story to music in 1829, based on Schiller's drama. The overture in particular is still well known today.
14387.m: Rossini wrote the opera about William Tell.

14388.q: What did Tell have to shoot off his son's head in the legend?
14388.e: The bailiff Gessler forced Tell to shoot an apple off his son's head with the crossbow. Tell hit the apple.
14388.m: Tell shot the apple off his son's head.

14389.q: In which place is the famous Tell monument from 1895?
14389.e: The monument shows Tell with his son. It stands in the village square of Altdorf, the capital of the canton of Uri.
14389.m: The Tell monument is in Altdorf.

14390.q: When did the Battle of Morgarten take place?
14390.e: The Battle of Morgarten took place on 15 November 1315. According to tradition, it was the first big fight of the young alliance against the Habsburgs.
14390.m: The Battle of Morgarten was on 15 November 1315.

14391.q: Who did the people of Schwyz fight against in the Battle of Morgarten?
14391.e: Duke Leopold I of Austria marched against Schwyz with a Habsburg army of knights. He managed to flee after the defeat.
14391.m: At Morgarten, the people of Schwyz defeated a Habsburg army of knights.

14392.q: What did the people of Schwyz quarrel about with Einsiedeln Abbey for a long time before the Battle of Morgarten?
14392.e: The people of Schwyz and Einsiedeln Abbey quarrelled for a long time over pastures and borders. After the people of Schwyz raided the abbey, the Habsburgs stepped in as its protectors.
14392.m: A quarrel over pastures with Einsiedeln Abbey led to the Battle of Morgarten.

14393.q: On which lake is the area of the Battle of Morgarten?
14393.e: The battle took place by Lake Ägeri on the border between Zug and Schwyz. But the exact spot is still not completely certain today.
14393.m: The Battle of Morgarten took place by Lake Ägeri.

14394.q: How did the people of Schwyz defeat the larger army of knights at Morgarten?
a: With an ambush at a narrow spot
In an open battle on a plain
With a long siege of a castle
14394.e: The knights were travelling on a narrow path between the mountain and the lake. There the people of Schwyz attacked by surprise, and the riders could hardly move.
14394.m: At Morgarten, the people of Schwyz used the narrow ground for an ambush.

14395.q: Which weapon of the Confederates does the chronicler mention as especially dangerous at the Battle of Morgarten?
14395.e: John of Winterthur calls the halberds, which were new at the time, terrible weapons of murder. With them, foot soldiers could attack riders.
14395.m: The halberd was a typical weapon of the Confederates.

14396.q: Why do you have to read old reports about the Battle of Morgarten carefully?
a: They were written later and embellished
There are photos that show something else
14396.e: The most important report comes from the monk John of Winterthur and was written decades after the battle. It is heavily embellished.
14396.m: Old chronicles about Morgarten are often embellished.

14397.q: What did Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden do a few weeks after the victory at Morgarten?
a: They founded the town of Zurich
14397.e: In December 1315, the three lands renewed their alliance in Brunnen. This alliance was closer than the Federal Charter of 1291.
14397.m: After Morgarten, the three lands renewed their alliance in 1315.

14398.q: The Federal Charter of 1291 is written in Latin. In which language did the Confederates write the Pact of Brunnen in 1315?
14398.e: The Pact of Brunnen from December 1315 is the first Confederate alliance in German. This way, more people could understand it.
14398.m: The Pact of Brunnen is the first Confederate alliance in German.

14399.q: What commemorates the Battle of Morgarten by Lake Ägeri today?
14399.e: The Morgarten monument was unveiled in 1908. It commemorates the battle of 1315.
14399.m: A monument by Lake Ägeri commemorates the Battle of Morgarten.

14400.q: When did the Battle of Sempach take place?
14400.e: The Battle of Sempach was on 9 July 1386. It was the most important fight in the Sempach War.
14400.m: The Battle of Sempach took place on 9 July 1386.

14401.q: What happened to the Habsburg duke Leopold III in the Battle of Sempach?
a: He went over to the Confederates
14401.e: Duke Leopold III joined the fighting himself and was killed. He was buried in a monastery in Aargau.
14401.m: Duke Leopold III lost his life at Sempach.

14402.q: In which present-day canton is Sempach?
14402.e: Sempach lies on Lake Sempach in the canton of Lucerne. The town had allied itself with Lucerne, which made the conflict with Habsburg worse.
14402.m: Sempach is in the canton of Lucerne.

14403.q: Which places fought on the Confederate side at Sempach?
14403.e: Lucerne and the three lands of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden fought on the Confederate side. Together they defeated Duke Leopold III's army.
14403.m: At Sempach, Lucerne and the three forest cantons won.

14404.q: Which hero, according to tradition, grabbed several enemy lances at Sempach and so opened a gap?
14404.e: According to tradition, Winkelried grabbed the knights' lances and sacrificed himself for his comrades. Whether this really happened has not been proven.
14404.m: Arnold Winkelried is the legendary hero of Sempach.

14405.q: Why is Winkelried's heroic deed not historically certain?
a: He is only named in chronicles long after the battle
He fought on the Habsburg side
14405.e: A Zurich chronicle from 1476 only mentions a nameless “loyal man”. Aegidius Tschudi is the first to name him, in the 16th century.
14405.m: The Winkelried story was only written down much later.

14406.q: What commemorates the battle at the battlefield near Sempach?
a: A battle chapel with a yearly memorial ceremony
14406.e: The battle chapel stands on the battlefield. A memorial ceremony has been held there every year since the later 15th century.
14406.m: The battle chapel near Sempach commemorates the battle of 1386.

14407.q: About how big was the Habsburg army at Sempach?
14407.e: The Habsburg army is estimated at about 4000 men, including many knights. The Confederates probably had 1500 to 2000 fighters.
14407.m: At Sempach, the Confederates won against a larger army.

14408.q: Which battle did the people of Glarus win against Habsburg two years after Sempach?
14408.e: In 1388, the people of Glarus, with support, defeated a Habsburg army at Näfels. This practically ended the Sempach War.
14408.m: After Sempach, the people of Glarus won at Näfels in 1388.

14409.q: What was the result of the victory at Sempach?
a: Habsburg power in the region was greatly weakened
The Confederates became part of France
Lucerne was handed over to the Habsburgs
14409.e: The victory secured the survival of the Confederation. After that, the Habsburgs lost more and more land and influence in the region.
14409.m: After Sempach, Habsburg power in what is now Switzerland grew weaker and weaker.

14410.q: Which town joined the alliance of the Confederates in 1332 as the first town?
14410.e: In 1332, Lucerne allied itself with Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden. For the first time, a town joined the rural lands.
14410.m: In 1332, Lucerne was the first town in the Confederate alliance.

14411.q: In which year did Zurich join the Confederate alliance?
14411.e: Zurich made an alliance with the forest cantons in 1351. The rich trading town made the Confederation stronger.
14411.m: Zurich became part of the Confederation in 1351.

14412.q: Which place joined in 1353 as the last of the Eight Old Cantons?
14412.e: With the alliance with Bern in 1353, the Confederation of eight places was complete. This period lasted until 1481.
14412.m: With Bern, the Eight Old Cantons were complete in 1353.

14413.q: Which of these places already belonged to the Eight Old Cantons?
14413.e: The Eight Old Cantons were Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Lucerne, Zurich, Glarus, Zug and Bern. Fribourg, Solothurn and Basel only joined later.
14413.m: Zug is one of the Eight Old Cantons of the Confederation.

14414.q: What did the Sempach Covenant of 1393 regulate?
a: How troops should behave in war
The election of a shared king
14414.e: The Sempach Covenant was a shared set of rules for war. It banned looting without permission and required churches, monasteries and women to be spared.
14414.m: In 1393, the Sempach Covenant set out the first shared rules for war.

14415.q: What was a condominium (Gemeine Herrschaft) in the Old Swiss Confederacy?
a: An area that several places ruled together
An area that belonged to the Pope
An area where only nobles lived
14415.e: Condominiums were subject territories that several Confederate places ran together. One example is Thurgau, which was ruled jointly from 1460.
14415.m: Condominiums were ruled jointly by several places.

14416.q: Which two places mainly fought each other in the Old Zurich War from 1440?
14416.e: Zurich and Schwyz quarrelled over the inheritance of the Counts of Toggenburg. This turned into a war among the Confederates.
14416.m: In the Old Zurich War, Zurich fought against Schwyz and the other places.

14417.q: Who did Zurich ally itself with against the other Confederates in the Old Zurich War?
14417.e: In 1442, Zurich made an alliance with the Habsburg king Frederick III. The other places saw this as betrayal, and the war became harsher.
14417.m: In the Old Zurich War, Zurich was for a time on Habsburg's side.

14418.q: How did the Battle of St Jakob an der Birs in 1444 end for the Confederates?
a: They lost, but the enemy withdrew
There was no fighting at all
They went on to conquer Paris
14418.e: The Confederates fought near Basel against a much larger French army of mercenaries, the Armagnacs. They lost, but the army then withdrew.
14418.m: At St Jakob an der Birs in 1444, the Confederates lost, but the enemy withdrew.

14419.q: What was the assembly called where envoys of the Confederate places met?
14419.e: At the Federal Diet (Tagsatzung), envoys of the places discussed shared questions. At that time there was no capital or government for everyone.
14419.m: The Federal Diet was the meeting of the envoys of all the places.

14420.q: In which period did the Burgundian Wars take place?
14420.e: The Burgundian Wars lasted from 1474 to 1477. They ended with the death of the Duke of Burgundy.
14420.m: The Burgundian Wars lasted from 1474 to 1477.

14421.q: Which ruler did the Confederates fight against in the Burgundian Wars?
14421.e: Charles the Bold was Duke of Burgundy and wanted to build a great empire. The Confederates and their allies stood up to him.
14421.m: Charles the Bold was the great enemy in the Burgundian Wars.

14422.q: What did the Confederates capture after the Battle of Grandson in 1476?
a: The crown of the King of France
14422.e: After the victory at Grandson, the Confederates captured the camp of Charles the Bold. The Burgundian booty with cannons, tents and valuables was famous.
14422.m: The Burgundian booty from Grandson was huge.

14423.q: How does the well-known Swiss saying continue: “At Grandson his treasure, at Murten his courage, ...”?
14423.e: The saying sums up what Charles the Bold lost: his treasure at Grandson, his courage at Murten and his life at Nancy in 1477.
14423.m: Charles the Bold lost his life at Nancy.

14424.q: In which battle did Charles the Bold die?
14424.e: On 5 January 1477 Charles the Bold was killed at Nancy in Lorraine. Swiss Confederate mercenaries fought there for Duke René of Lorraine.
14424.m: Charles the Bold fell at Nancy in 1477.

14425.q: Which country gave the Swiss Confederates money to fight Burgundy?
14425.e: King Louis XI of France wanted to weaken Burgundy without going to war himself. He paid the Confederates.
14425.m: France paid the Confederates to fight Burgundy.

14426.q: Which royal house gained a large part of Burgundy through a marriage after the death of Charles the Bold?
14426.e: Charles’s daughter Mary married Maximilian of Habsburg in 1477. This is how a lot of Burgundian land passed to the Habsburgs.
14426.m: A large part of Burgundy went to the Habsburgs.

14427.q: Which member of the Swiss Confederation pushed the Burgundian Wars forward most strongly?
14427.e: Bern wanted to extend its power to the west and led the Confederates. Together with Fribourg, Bern conquered parts of Vaud in 1475.
14427.m: Bern was the driving force in the Burgundian Wars.

14428.q: Which town did Bern and Fribourg govern together after the Burgundian Wars?
14428.e: Murten, Grandson, Orbe and Echallens became lordships shared by Bern and Fribourg.
14428.m: Murten was governed jointly by Bern and Fribourg.

14429.q: What was a result of the victories in the Burgundian Wars for the Swiss fighters?
a: They were in great demand as mercenaries in Europe
They were no longer allowed to carry weapons
They had to live in Burgundy
14429.e: The victories made the Swiss foot soldiers famous all over Europe. Afterwards many princes wanted to hire them as mercenaries, known as Reisläufer.
14429.m: After the Burgundian Wars Swiss mercenaries were highly sought after.

14430.q: Which two members joined the Swiss Confederation in 1481?
14430.e: Fribourg and Solothurn were admitted in 1481. This ended the period of the Eight Old Cantons.
14430.m: Fribourg and Solothurn joined the Confederation in 1481.

14431.q: Which agreement settled the dispute between the town cantons and the rural cantons in 1481?
14431.e: Towns and rural cantons argued about admitting Fribourg and Solothurn and about the booty from Burgundy. The Covenant of Stans of 1481 brought an agreement.
14431.m: The Covenant of Stans prevented the Confederation from breaking apart in 1481.

14432.q: Which hermit is said to have helped reach the agreement in Stans in 1481 with his advice?
14432.e: Niklaus von Flüe, known as Brother Klaus, lived as a hermit in the Ranft. His advice helped to settle the quarrel among the Confederates in 1481.
14432.m: Brother Klaus helped to reconcile the Confederates in 1481.

14433.q: Which two members joined the Swiss Confederation in 1501?
14433.e: After the Swabian War, Basel and Schaffhausen joined in 1501. They became the 11th and 12th members.
14433.m: Basel and Schaffhausen became part of the Confederation in 1501.

14434.q: Which member was admitted in 1513 as the thirteenth?
14434.e: Appenzell became a full member in 1513. After that, no more members with equal rights were admitted until 1798.
14434.m: With Appenzell there were thirteen members from 1513.

14436.q: What did the Peace of Basel in 1499 mean for the Swiss Confederation?
a: It was practically independent of the Empire
It had to give Basel to the Habsburgs
14436.e: After the Peace of Basel, the reforms and courts of the Empire no longer applied in the Confederation. Legally, however, it remained part of the Empire until 1648.
14436.m: From 1499 the Confederation was practically independent.

14438.q: What was an associate of the Swiss Confederation (Zugewandter Ort)?
a: An ally without an equal say
A town that belonged to a foreign country
A monastery owned by the Diet
14438.e: Associates were allied with the Confederates but did not have all the rights of a full member. Examples are Valais and the town of St Gallen.
14438.m: Associates were allies without full rights.

14439.q: Which event ended the Old Swiss Confederation of thirteen members in 1798?
a: The invasion of French troops and the Helvetic Republic
The founding of the federal state
14439.e: In 1798 French troops marched in. The Old Swiss Confederation came to an end and the Helvetic Republic was created.
14439.m: With the Helvetic Republic the Old Swiss Confederation ended in 1798.

14440.q: When did the Battle of Marignano take place?
14440.e: The battle lasted two days, from 13 to 14 September 1515. It was part of the Italian Wars.
14440.m: The Battle of Marignano was in September 1515.

14441.q: Marignano, today called Melegnano, lies near which city?
14441.e: Marignano lies south-east of Milan in Lombardy. The fight was about who would rule the Duchy of Milan.
14441.m: Marignano is near Milan in Italy.

14442.q: Which king defeated the Swiss Confederates at Marignano?
14442.e: The young French king Francis I wanted to win back the duchy in northern Italy. He defeated the Confederates at Marignano.
14442.m: Francis I of France defeated the Confederates in 1515.

14443.q: How long did the Battle of Marignano last?
14443.e: The battle lasted from 13 to 14 September 1515. On the second day the French received help from Venice.
14443.m: The Battle of Marignano lasted two days.

14444.q: Which territory did the Confederates and France fight over at Marignano?
14444.e: France and the Confederates both wanted to rule the rich Duchy of Milan. At Marignano France won.

14445.q: Why were troops from Bern, Fribourg and Solothurn missing at Marignano?
a: They had accepted a French peace offer and left
They had to fight against Burgundy
They had not found the way across the Alps
14445.e: Shortly before the battle these members accepted a French offer in the Treaty of Gallarate. Around 10,000 men left, including men from Biel and Valais, which weakened the Confederates.
14445.m: Before Marignano the Confederates were divided among themselves.

14446.q: According to later estimates, roughly how many Confederates died at Marignano?
14446.e: Later estimates put the number of Confederate dead at about 9,000 to 10,000. Several thousand soldiers also died on the French side.
14446.m: Marignano was a defeat with very heavy losses for the Confederates.

14447.q: Which treaty did the Confederates make with France in 1516?
14447.e: On 29 November 1516 the Confederates and France made the Perpetual Peace. Afterwards France was allowed to recruit mercenaries in the Confederation.
14447.m: After Marignano the Confederates made the Perpetual Peace with France in 1516.

14448.q: Which areas south of the Alps were the Confederates allowed to keep for the most part after the peace of 1516?
14448.e: The Confederates kept their conquests in today’s Ticino but had to give up the Ossola valley. These areas were governed as subject territories.
14448.m: After Marignano most of Ticino stayed with the Confederates.

14449.q: What is the Battle of Marignano often seen as a turning point for?
a: The end of Swiss wars of conquest
The start of the Reformation in Bern
The founding of the federal state
14449.e: After Marignano the Confederates no longer conquered large territories. Many see this as the beginning of their later restraint in wars, although mercenary service continued.
14449.m: After Marignano the Confederates no longer pursued their own policy of conquest.

a: A new start for the Church
14450.e: Renaissance comes from French and means “rebirth”. It refers to the rediscovery of the art and knowledge of antiquity.
14450.m: Renaissance means the rebirth of antiquity.

14451.q: In which country did the Renaissance begin?
14451.e: The Renaissance began in Italy in the 14th and 15th centuries. There were rich cities there and many remains from Roman antiquity.
14451.m: The Renaissance has its origins in Italy.

14452.q: Which city is considered the cradle of the Renaissance?
14452.e: In Florence, rich bankers and merchants supported artists and scholars. Many of the first great works of the Renaissance were created there.
14452.m: Florence was the centre of the early Renaissance.

14453.q: Which rich banking family supported many artists in Florence?
14453.e: The Medici were bankers and ruled Florence for a long time. They gave artists such as Botticelli big commissions.
14453.m: The Medici made Florence a city of art.

14454.q: What do you call a person who supports artists with money and commissions?
14454.e: A patron supports art and science with their wealth. In the Renaissance, princes, popes and rich merchants were important patrons.
14454.m: A patron supports artists with their money.

14455.q: Which era did the people of the Renaissance want to bring back to life?
14455.e: The people of the Renaissance admired the art, buildings and writings of the ancient Greeks and Romans. This period is called antiquity.

14456.q: Which painting technique, developed in the Renaissance, makes pictures look deep and three-dimensional?
14456.e: In linear perspective, all lines meet at one vanishing point. This makes pictures look like a view into a real space.

14457.q: Which master builder created the great dome of Florence Cathedral?
14457.e: Filippo Brunelleschi built the huge dome without a conventional supporting scaffold. The cathedral was consecrated in 1436.
14457.m: Brunelleschi built the dome of Florence Cathedral.

14458.q: Which painter created the famous picture “The Birth of Venus”?
14458.e: Sandro Botticelli painted “The Birth of Venus” in Florence. The picture shows a goddess from ancient legend.
14458.m: Botticelli painted The Birth of Venus.

14459.q: Which Renaissance painter created the wall painting “The School of Athens” in the Vatican?
14459.e: Raphael painted “The School of Athens” in the Vatican. The picture shows famous ancient thinkers such as Plato and Aristotle.
14459.m: Raphael painted The School of Athens.

14460.q: Which invention by Johannes Gutenberg helped to spread the new ideas of the Renaissance quickly?
14460.e: Around 1450 in Mainz, Gutenberg invented printing with movable metal letters. Books could now be made much faster and more cheaply.
14460.m: Printing spread knowledge quickly across Europe.

14461.q: Which German artist brought Renaissance ideas from Italy to Nuremberg?
14461.e: Albrecht Dürer travelled to Italy and got to know the new art there. Among his famous works are his self-portrait and the “Young Hare”.
14461.m: Albrecht Dürer brought the Renaissance to Germany.

14462.q: Which Renaissance painter worked for a long time in Basel before becoming court painter in England?
14462.e: Hans Holbein the Younger lived and painted in Basel for many years. Later he became court painter to the English King Henry VIII.
14462.m: Hans Holbein the Younger painted in Basel and London.

14463.q: What is meant by a Renaissance “universal genius”?
a: A person who achieves great things in many fields
A king who rules many countries
A monk who copies many books
A trader who travels all over the world
14463.e: The Renaissance ideal was the all-round educated person. Leonardo da Vinci, for example, was a painter, inventor and researcher all at once.
14463.m: A universal genius is gifted in many fields.

14464.q: Which Florentine wrote the book “The Prince” about power and politics?
14464.e: Niccolò Machiavelli wrote “The Prince” around 1513. The book explains plainly how a ruler gains and keeps power.

14467.q: Which city fell to the Ottomans in 1453, after which Greek scholars came to Italy?
14467.e: In 1453 the Ottomans conquered Constantinople. Greek scholars with old manuscripts had already been coming to Italy, but now even more came.
14467.m: After the fall of Constantinople, scholars came to Italy.

14468.q: Which sculptor of the early Renaissance created a famous bronze statue of David?
14468.e: Donatello made a bronze David in Florence. It was one of the first free-standing nude statues since antiquity.
14468.m: Donatello was a great sculptor of the early Renaissance.

14469.q: In which two centuries was the Renaissance at its height in Europe?
14469.e: The Renaissance began in Italy in the 14th century and reached its peak in the 15th and 16th centuries. It forms the transition from the Middle Ages to the modern era.
14469.m: The Renaissance flourished in the 15th and 16th centuries.

14470.q: What was at the centre of humanism?
14470.e: The word humanism comes from the Latin “humanus”, meaning human. Humanists wanted to improve people through education and ancient writings.
14470.m: In humanism, people are at the centre.

14471.q: What does the humanists’ motto “ad fontes” mean?
14471.e: Humanists wanted to read the old texts in the original, instead of only in later copies and interpretations. “Ad fontes” means “to the sources”.
14471.m: “Ad fontes” means back to the sources.

14472.q: In which country did humanism begin in the 14th century?
14472.e: Italian scholars such as Francesco Petrarca searched for old Roman texts. From Italy, humanism spread all over Europe.

14473.q: Which two ancient languages did humanists learn especially eagerly?
14473.e: The most important writings of antiquity were written in Latin and Greek. Humanists wanted to read them in the original.

14474.q: Which famous humanist lived in Basel for a long time and died there in 1536?
14474.e: Erasmus of Rotterdam worked closely with printers in Basel. He died in Basel in 1536 and is buried in Basel Minster.
14474.m: Erasmus of Rotterdam worked and died in Basel.

14475.q: Which book did Erasmus publish in a new Greek edition in Basel in 1516?
14475.e: In 1516 in Basel, Erasmus published the New Testament in Greek with a new Latin translation. Luther used the second edition of 1519 for his translation of the Bible.
14475.m: Erasmus published the Greek New Testament in Basel.

14476.q: Why was Basel a centre of humanism in the 16th century?
a: It had a university and many printing workshops
It was the seat of the Emperor
It was right by the sea
14476.e: Basel had a university and many important printing workshops. That is why many scholars came to the city to teach and to have their books printed.
14476.m: Its university and printers made Basel a centre of humanism.

14477.q: In which year was the University of Basel, the oldest in Switzerland, founded?
14477.e: The University of Basel opened in 1460. It is the oldest university in present-day Switzerland.
14477.m: Founded in 1460, the University of Basel is the oldest in Switzerland.

14478.q: Which invention helped to spread the ideas of humanism quickly?
14478.e: With printing, books could be made quickly and in large numbers. That way the humanists’ writings reached many readers.
14478.m: Printing spread the ideas of humanism.

14479.q: Which Zurich reformer was strongly influenced by the humanist Erasmus?
14479.e: Huldrych Zwingli read the writings of Erasmus and learned Greek to read the Bible in the original. In this way humanism shaped his Reformation in Zurich.
14479.m: Zwingli was a humanist and reformer in Zurich.

14480.q: What does the word “utopia”, which goes back to a book from 1516, mean?
14480.e: In “Utopia”, Thomas More described an invented island with an ideal society. Today such a dream of an ideal world is called a utopia.
14480.m: A utopia is an imagined ideal world.

14481.q: Which subjects were especially important to the humanists?
14481.e: Humanists studied grammar, rhetoric, poetry, history and philosophy. They called these subjects the “studia humanitatis”.
14481.m: Humanists studied languages, poetry and history.

14482.q: Where did humanists often search for forgotten ancient manuscripts?
14482.e: Many ancient texts had been copied and kept in monasteries. Humanists such as Poggio Bracciolini found valuable manuscripts there, for example at the Abbey of St Gallen.
14482.m: Humanists found old texts in monastery libraries.

14483.q: Which Swiss story was made especially well known by the chronicle of Aegidius Tschudi?
14483.e: Aegidius Tschudi wrote a large chronicle of the Swiss Confederation. His account of William Tell shaped Switzerland’s view of its history for a long time.
14483.m: Tschudi’s chronicle shaped the Tell story.

14484.q: What did the Zurich scholar Conrad Gessner describe in a huge work in the 16th century?
a: All the battles of the Confederates
